title: Enhancing Multi-Modal LLMs Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Group Normalization
claim: Std-normalization amplifies advantages for extreme easy and hard samples, while medium-difficulty samples keep balanced advantages.
layout: 3 rows by 3 columns, left-to-right: sample, reward bars, advantage curve
description: A 3x3 grid. Each row is a difficulty level, with a colored header on the left: green Easy, yellow Medium, orange Hard. Column headers read Easy/Medium/Hard, Reward, and Advantage distribution. Each row starts with a photo and a dashed speech-bubble question: a cow on grass, a microwave above a pot, and a boy at a whiteboard math problem. The middle column is a light-blue bar chart of eight binary rewards between 0 and 1. Easy has nearly all ones, Medium is mixed, and Hard has nearly all zeros. The right column is a blue density curve annotated with std values and axis extremes. Easy and Hard have sharp, narrow spikes (std=0.33, extreme values -2.64 or 2.64), while Medium has a flat, wide bump (std=0.5, values around ±0.5). The eye goes first to the colored headers and the contrast between the spiky and flat curves.
caption: The advantage distribution after the normalization of reward varies among samples. Extreme samples like easy and hard ones are amplified after std-normalization, whereas medium samples exhibit more balanced advantages.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) have significantly advanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models. Extending these methods to multimodal settings, however, faces a critical challenge: the instability of std-based normalization, which is easily distorted by extreme samples with nearly positive or negative rewards. Unlike pure-text LLMs, multimodal models are particularly sensitive to such distortions, as both perceptual and reasoning errors influence their responses. To address this, we characterize each sample by its difficulty, defined through perceptual complexity (measured via visual entropy) and reasoning uncertainty (captured by model confidence). Building on this characterization, we propose difficulty-aware group normalization (Durian), which re-groups samples by difficulty levels and shares the std within each group. Our approach preserves GRPO's intra-group distinctions while eliminating sensitivity to extreme cases, yielding significant performance gains across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
